question: My lease says no pets. Can my landlord evict me for having a cat?
correct_answer: A lease term banning animals in the residential complex is void, so the 'no pets' clause itself can't be enforced.
assistant_answer:
That sounds stressful. Here is what the law says.

**A "no pets" clause in your lease does not, on its own, let your landlord evict you.** Under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a lease provision that bans animals in the residential complex is void (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 14).

**An eviction based on an animal has to meet specific conditions.** If the landlord applies to the Board to evict you because of an animal, the Board cannot order eviction unless it is satisfied that you keep the animal and that one of these is true (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 76(1)):

- **(a)** Past behaviour of animals of that species has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex for the landlord or other tenants.
- **(b)** The animal has caused the landlord or another tenant a serious allergic reaction.
- **(c)** The species or breed is inherently dangerous to the safety of the landlord or other tenants.

The Board also cannot evict you on ground (a) if it is satisfied that your animal did not cause or contribute to the interference. It also cannot evict you on ground (b) if it is satisfied your animal did not cause or contribute to the allergic reaction (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 76(2) and (3)).

**Steps a landlord must follow.** For a cause-based eviction, a landlord may give a notice of termination if a tenant's conduct substantially interferes with others' reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. The notice must give a termination date at least 20 days after it is given and require the tenant to stop the conduct within seven days. If the tenant stops within those seven days, the notice is void (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 64(1) to (3)). The landlord can then apply to the Board, generally within 30 days after the termination date in the notice (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 69(1), (2)).

**The Board's discretion.** Even when a landlord applies, the Board can refuse the eviction if it is satisfied that refusing would be fair, based on all the circumstances (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 83(1)(a)).

question: When do I get paid overtime?
correct_answer: For each hour worked over 44 hours in a work week, at least one and a half times the regular rate.

- **Regular rate:** If you're paid by the hour, your regular rate is what you earn for an hour in your usual work week, not counting overtime hours. - **Two or more regular rates:** If you have two or more regular rates with the same employer in a week, overtime starts once your total hours reach the threshold. Each overtime hour is paid at one and one-half times the rate for the work done in that hour (s. 22(1.1)).
- **Hours averaged over weeks:** Hours can be averaged over two or more weeks, but only if you made an agreement with your employer to do so. The averaging period cannot exceed four weeks or the number of weeks in the agreement, whichever is shorter (s. 22(2)).
- **Time off instead of pay:** Instead of overtime pay, you can get one and one-half hours of paid time off for each overtime hour, if you and your employer agree. The time off must be taken within three months of the work week, or within 12 months with your agreement (s. 22(7)).
- **Public holidays:** Hours you work on a public holiday and receive premium pay for are not counted toward overtime (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 31).
- **Hotels, restaurants and similar businesses:** For employees who work 24 weeks or less in a calendar year at these businesses and get room and board, overtime starts after 50 hours in a week (O. Reg. 285/01, s. 14).
- **Highway transport:** Certain truck drivers get overtime after 60 hours in a week (O. Reg. 285/01, s. 18(1)–(2)).
- **Waiting time:** Time you are required to stay at work while waiting or ready to be called to work, or during a rest break other than an eating period, can count as work (O. Reg. 285/01, s. 1.1(1)(b)). Certain breaks and time off are not counted (s. 1.1(2)).

question: Do I get paid extra if I work on a public holiday?
correct_answer: If you agree to work a public holiday, the employer must either pay your regular rate for the hours worked and give you a substitute day off with public holiday pay, or, if you both agree, pay public holiday pay plus premium pay (at least 1.5 times your regular rate) for each hour worked.
assistant_answer:
Often, yes. The law gives extra pay in two main ways, depending on how you came to work the holiday.

**If your employer requires you to work** (only in a hospital, a continuous operation, or a hotel, motel, tourist resort, restaurant or tavern), the employer must choose one of these:
- **Option A:** Pay your regular rate for the hours worked on the holiday, and give you a substitute day off. You also get public holiday pay for that substitute day. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 28(2)(a))
- **Option B:** Pay public holiday pay for the day, plus premium pay for each hour worked. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 28(2)(b))

**If you and your employer agree** that you will work the holiday, the same two options apply. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 27(2)). Under Option B, the agreement must also say so. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 27(2)(b)) For a holiday that falls on a day you wouldn't normally work, or on a vacation day, the same rules apply under a separate agreement. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 30(1), s. 30(2))

**How much is premium pay?** It must be at least one and one-half times your regular rate. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 24(2))

**Other points:**
- Public holiday pay is generally based on your regular wages and vacation pay in the four work weeks before the holiday, divided by 20. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 24(1))
- Hours worked on a public holiday with premium pay do not count toward overtime. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 31)
- If you are scheduled to work but don't, you may lose some or all of these entitlements unless you had reasonable cause. - An employee may refuse to work on a public holiday. If an employee has agreed to work, they may still decline, but only with at least 48 hours' notice. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 73(1), s. 73(3))

question: I took out a payday loan yesterday. Can I still cancel it?
correct_answer: Yes. A borrower can cancel a payday loan agreement without any reason up to the end of the second day after getting the agreement (or the next day the lender is open, if it is closed that day), by giving notice. The lender must then refund the payments and return post-dated cheques and debit authorizations; the borrower repays the advance.
assistant_answer:
Under the law, you may be able to cancel without giving a reason, but only within a short window. A borrower may cancel a payday loan agreement without any reason up to the end of the second day after the lender complies with subsections 29(1) and (2), if the lender is open for business that day. If the lender is closed that day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open (Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 30(1)).

If you received the loan and a copy of the agreement yesterday, the second day after that would be tomorrow, provided the lender is open then. The sections don't say exactly when the lender "complies" with its requirements, so the exact deadline depends on those facts.

To cancel, the law says:

- **Give notice in time.** The notice goes to the lender, or to the loan broker if one helped you get the loan (O. Reg. 98/09, s. 19(1); Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 30(2)).
- **Repay the advance.** At the time you give notice, you must repay the amount you borrowed (O. Reg. 98/09, s. 19(2); Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 43(3)(b)).
- **The cancellation takes effect** when you give notice, and it cancels the agreement as if it never existed (Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 43(1), (2)).
- **The lender must refund any payments you made** under the agreement, except repayments of the advance itself. It must also return or destroy post-dated cheques and pre-authorized debits, depending on their form (Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 43(3)(a)). The lender must do this at the earliest reasonable opportunity after you give notice (O. Reg. 98/09, s. 19(3)).

Separately, if the lender did not give you the loan or a copy of a compliant agreement when you signed, the law says you only have to repay the advance and do not have to pay the cost of borrowing (Payday Loans Act, 2008, s. 29(4)).
